THE APPRENTICESHIP AGREEMENT / HOW WE WORK

Take the work seriously. Give the process a chance.

This apprenticeship can create real value, but the value depends on what each person brings to it.

THE ITINERARY STAYS INTACT.

The learning roadmap and sequence remain our shared reference point, even when a session, delivery detail or plan has to change. We may adjust logistics; we will communicate those changes. We do not abandon the learning journey every time something shifts.

COMMIT TO THE PROCESS.

Show up, participate, complete the work and communicate early when something affects your ability to take part. Consistency gives the learning time to compound.

READ BEYOND THE SLIDES.

Do your self-reading. Follow useful sources. Ask questions. Explore tools and examples independently. Curiosity is part of the job, not extra credit.

BRING A ZEAL TO WIN.

Be ambitious about your progress and generous with other people's. Take feedback seriously, improve your work and keep raising your standard.

RESPECT THE ROOM.

Be punctual, constructive and professional. Disagree with ideas thoughtfully. Do not share another participant's personal information or work outside the group without permission.

OWN YOUR DEVELOPMENT.

Ask for help when needed, but take responsibility for practising between sessions. Nobody can build your skill on your behalf.

WEEK 01 / HOW THE APPRENTICESHIP RUNS

Two classes. One working week.

Every week has two live classes. The first builds your foundation. The second puts that learning to work.

CLASS 01 / LEARN THE BASICSWe introduce the week's subject, core concepts, rules, frameworks and terminology. This is where you learn the language of the work and understand what good practice looks like.
BETWEEN CLASSES / DO THE WORKReview the lesson, read beyond the slides, complete the exercises and develop your assignment. Bring questions and evidence to the second class.
CLASS 02 / REVIEW AND REFINEWe assess your assignments, discuss your decisions, work through feedback and study visual inspirations and relevant examples. You leave knowing what to improve and how to apply it.
BY FRIDAY / PUBLISH YOUR ARTICLESubmit your article no later than Friday. It should connect to the week's learning and be ready to publish on your LinkedIn profile that same week. Late submissions may miss that week's publishing window.
LINKEDIN CONNECTIONS Share your LinkedIn profile in the Marketing Apprenticeship group, not in this workbook. Connect with your cohort there, follow one another and support each other's articles with thoughtful engagement.
WEEK 01 ASSESSMENT: The assessment is built into this workbook. Complete the practice and assignment sections near the end, then use the second class to review your work and receive feedback.

THE AI QUESTION

If AI can do the work, what are we paying you for?

AI can help generate options, analyse information and speed up execution. A marketer still has to frame the right problem, judge the quality of evidence, understand context, choose a direction and own the consequences.

AI can accelerate

Drafting research questions, organising notes, summarising source material, generating options and spotting themes worth checking.

You remain accountable for

Choosing the problem, validating sources, interpreting context, making trade-offs and owning the recommendation.

The tool can produce an answer. You are responsible for the decision.

WHAT CONTENT MARKETING MEANS NOW

Content gives people a reason to pay attention before they are ready to buy.

Content marketing is the planned creation and distribution of useful, relevant or entertaining material that attracts a defined audience, earns attention and supports a business objective over time.

EDUCATE

Explain a problem, teach a skill, answer a question or help someone make a better decision.

Guides · explainers · newsletters · webinars
DEMONSTRATE

Show the product, process, expertise or result in a way people can evaluate.

Product demos · walkthroughs · case examples
BUILD CULTURE

Give people language, shared references and reasons to participate.

Community stories · creator content · conversations
CREATE CONVICTION

Address objections, show proof and make the value easier to understand.

Testimonials · comparisons · founder perspectives
WHY IT MATTERS

People research, compare, ask peers, watch demonstrations and form opinions before speaking to sales. Useful content helps a business become discoverable, understood, remembered and trusted during that process.

THE SACRIFICE

Content takes time, consistency and distribution. Publishing more is not the goal. Make fewer pieces that answer real questions and give each channel a job.

15 / 60
THE PEOPLE BEHIND THE WORK

Marketing is a team sport. The roles solve different problems.

Titles vary by company. These are functional responsibilities you will encounter across marketing teams, agencies and growing businesses.

BRAND / MARKETING STRATEGIST

Defines the business problem, audience, market position, brand direction and priorities. Connects research to decisions.

CONTENT STRATEGIST / EDITOR

Decides what the brand should say, to whom, why, in which formats and across which channels. Builds the editorial system.

CREATIVE STRATEGIST / DESIGNER

Turns the strategy into concepts, visual systems, campaigns, formats and creative assets that earn attention and communicate value.

MARKETING ASSISTANT / COORDINATOR

Keeps execution moving: scheduling, publishing, asset organisation, briefs, research admin, reporting support, coordination and follow-ups.

GROWTH / PERFORMANCE MARKETER

Runs experiments across acquisition, conversion and retention. Reads channel and funnel data, allocates spend and improves performance.

SALES / CLOSER

Works directly with qualified prospects, understands objections, manages the sales conversation and helps convert demand into revenue.

In a small company, one person may hold several of these responsibilities. The work still needs to happen, even when the job titles do not exist.

THE MODERN MARKETER'S WORKING FLUENCIES

Your value comes from how well you think, make and learn.

Tools change. These capabilities help a marketer make better decisions and produce work that has commercial value.

01BRAND PSYCHOLOGY

Understand perception, memory, trust, emotion, identity, social proof, choice architecture and the reasons people attach meaning to brands.

Ask: What makes this feel relevant, credible and worth choosing?
02WRITING

Turn complex ideas into language people understand and remember. Write positioning, briefs, hooks, scripts, emails, landing pages and sales messages.

Ask: What does the reader need to understand, feel or do?
03AI FLUENCY

Use AI to research, organise, ideate, prototype, produce and analyse. Give good context, check outputs and protect sensitive information.

Ask: What can I accelerate, and what still needs human judgement?
04DATA FLUENCY

Read analytics, understand metrics, diagnose funnel performance, compare results and distinguish correlation from a useful explanation.

Ask: What happened, why might it have happened, and what should change?
THE STANDARD: Strong marketers combine judgement with execution. Brand psychology without evidence becomes assumption. Data without context becomes noise. AI without direction produces volume.

YOUR PERSONAL BRAND IS PROFESSIONAL PROOF

Let people see how you think before they hire you.

A personal brand is the body of public evidence associated with your name: what you know, what you notice, how you work, what you make and the problems you can help solve.

SHOW YOUR THINKING

Share useful observations, breakdowns, opinions with reasoning, lessons from projects and the questions you ask.

SHOW YOUR WORK

Publish portfolio pieces, process notes, experiments, outcomes and the decisions behind the finished work.

SHOW YOUR RANGE

Demonstrate writing, research, creative judgement, data interpretation, collaboration and responsible AI use.

EGC
EMPLOYEE-GENERATED CONTENT

Companies increasingly have reasons to feature the people behind the brand: their expertise, perspective, process and personality. A marketer with a credible public voice can contribute to founder-led content, employee advocacy, recruiting and brand trust. It is an opportunity, not an obligation to turn every employee into an influencer.

Build a reputation around useful work. Do not confuse visibility with credibility.

HOW THE WORK CONNECTS / A FUNCTIONAL HIERARCHY

Think of marketing as a tree.

The work flows from strategic decisions into planning, creative production, operations and revenue. Each layer gives the next one direction.

BRAND STRATEGYNaming · Research · Positioning · Visual identityDefines who the brand is, who it serves, what it stands for and why it deserves to be chosen.
CONTENT STRATEGYAudience · Message · Editorial pillars · Channels · DistributionDecides what the brand needs to communicate, to whom, and where.
VISUAL EXECUTION / CREATIVE STRATEGYCampaign concepts · Art direction · Design · Video · FormatsTurns the message into work people can notice, understand and engage with.
MARKETING ASSISTANT / COORDINATIONScheduling · Publishing · Asset management · Admin · Reporting supportKeeps the system organised and the recurring work moving.
GROWTH MARKETER / SALES CLOSERAcquisition · Experiments · Lead nurturing · Conversion · Revenue feedbackTurns qualified attention into customers and feeds market response back into the system.
IMPORTANT: This is a hierarchy of strategic dependency, not a universal company org chart. Teams combine roles differently. The closer and growth marketer also feed customer objections, conversion data and market signals back up the tree.

BUSINESSES HAVE DIFFERENT OPERATING LOGIC

Different businesses need different marketing questions.

Classify a business across separate dimensions before deciding what marketing questions to ask: its sector and industry, the model through which it earns, the customer it serves, and the offer customers compare. The examples below show operating contexts, not mutually exclusive industry labels.

Product / retail

Investigate demand, product-market fit, pricing, merchandising, distribution, stock availability, conversion and repeat purchase.

One company can be in financial services, operate as a marketplace, sell to businesses and consumers, and compete in a specific payments category. Classify each dimension separately.

WHO IS THE CUSTOMER?

B2B, B2C or somewhere in between?

B2B businesses sell to organisations. B2C businesses sell to individual consumers. Hybrid models serve both, often with different offers, buying processes and decision-makers.

B2B

Organisations buy. Investigate the business need, decision-makers, approval process, procurement, contract value, sales cycle and implementation.

The person using the product may not be the person paying for it.

A marketing objective should answer a business need.

A business may need more qualified demand, higher conversion, repeat purchases, stronger distribution, product adoption, better reputation or a more reliable lead pipeline. The objective depends on the constraint.

DEMANDAttract more of the right people.
CONVERSIONHelp more qualified prospects buy.

34 / 60
THE COURTSHIP PRINCIPLE ♡

Getting attention is the beginning. What you do with it is the relationship.

Think about someone genuinely trying to court a woman's attention. He pays attention to what matters to her, remembers what she says, notices how she responds and makes an effort to show up well. A marketer should bring that same attentiveness to understanding and serving an audience.

Pay attention

Learn what people value, what they need, what they respond to and what makes them hesitate. Do not assume interest just because you want it.

Deliver on the effort

Make every interaction count. The product, service, communication and experience must live up to the promise that earned their attention.

The audience gets to choose. Your job is to understand, respect that choice and give people a good reason to stay.
35 / 60
SEGMENT BEFORE YOU GENERALISE

Your target audience is not everybody with a smartphone.

Segment people by meaningful differences: needs, behaviours, context, location, budget, urgency, usage and buying situation. A useful segment helps the business make a decision.

NEEDWhat outcome are they seeking?
BEHAVIOURHow do they currently act?
CONTEXTWhen and where does the need arise?
BUDGETWhat can they spend?
URGENCYHow soon do they need a solution?
USAGEHow do they use the offer?
If every person qualifies, the segment is too broad to guide much.
♡ THE COURTSHIP LENS A good courtship starts with knowing who you are trying to get to know. You cannot make a meaningful effort toward everybody at once.
36 / 60
WHO THEY ARE VS WHY THEY BUY

Demographics tell you who. They do not always tell you why.

Age, location, income and occupation can help describe an audience. Motivations, desired outcomes, habits, constraints and decision criteria help explain behaviour.

Who

Age, location, occupation, income, household or organisational context.

Why

Motivation, desired outcome, habits, fears, decision criteria and constraints.

Do not turn a demographic profile into a personality stereotype.
♡ THE COURTSHIP LENS Knowing her age or where she lives is a starting point. Paying attention means learning what matters to her and why.
37 / 60
UNDERSTAND THE JOB

What are customers trying to achieve when they buy?

Explore the task, frustration or aspiration behind the purchase. Ask what happened before they started looking, what alternatives they considered, and what a successful outcome would look like.

TRIGGER
What started the search?
PROGRESS
What are they trying to achieve?
CHOICE
What shapes the decision?
OUTCOME
What does success mean?
People buy progress, relief, convenience, status, confidence and many other outcomes. Find the one supported by evidence.
♡ THE COURTSHIP LENS Listen for the outcome she actually wants. Do not decide what would make her happy without asking and observing.
38 / 60
THE REASONS THEY HESITATE

What makes them choose, wait or walk away?

Investigate trust, price, timing, access, complexity, risk, social influence, previous experience and competing priorities. Objections often reveal what the business has failed to explain or solve.

TRUSTDo they believe the promise?
PRICECan they afford it, and does it feel worth it?
ACCESSCan they find, buy and receive it?
RISKWhat could go wrong for them?
TIMINGWhy now, or why later?
COMPLEXITYIs the process difficult?
A hesitation is information. Treat it as such.
♡ THE COURTSHIP LENS A pause is a response too. Find out whether the hesitation comes from price, trust, timing, access or a promise the business has not delivered on.

FOLLOW THE CUSTOMER'S EXPERIENCE

How does a customer move from discovery to purchase?

Trace what happens before someone knows the brand, while they compare options, at the point of purchase, during use and after the experience. Note the questions and friction at each point.

DISCOVERY
How did they hear?
CONSIDERATION
What do they compare?
PURCHASE
What helps them commit?
AFTER
What happens in use?
This is a customer journey map, not a campaign plan.
♡ THE COURTSHIP LENS The relationship is shaped by every interaction, not just the first impression. Pay attention to what happens after the yes.
40 / 60
BUILD FROM EVIDENCE

A persona is a research tool, not a fictional character sheet.

A useful audience profile summarises a real pattern in needs, behaviour, context, decision criteria and barriers. Include evidence and confidence level. Do not invent quotes or motivations to make the profile feel complete.

Include

Observed needs, behaviour, context, goals, decision criteria, barriers and supporting evidence.

Do not invent

Quotes, lifestyle details, attitudes or motivations that no source or participant supports.

If the evidence is thin, label the profile as a hypothesis.
♡ THE COURTSHIP LENS Remember what people actually told you. A thoughtful marketer keeps receipts, not invented details about a person they have never met.
41 / 60

Build audience segments from evidence.

Identify groups with meaningfully different needs, motivations, buying behaviour or barriers. Do not segment people using demographics alone.

SEGMENT

Give the group a useful working label. What makes this group distinct?

NEED / JOB

What are they trying to achieve or solve?

BUYING TRIGGER

What situation makes them start looking for a solution?

DECISION FACTORS

What influences their choice: price, trust, speed, status, convenience, proof or something else?

BARRIERS

What makes them delay, reject or abandon the purchase?

EVIDENCE

Where did this information come from? What still needs validation?

Use interviews, reviews, customer comments, search behaviour and credible market sources. Do not invent customer quotes.
♡ THE COURTSHIP LENS Turn what you have learned into distinct groups and useful decisions. Show what you know, where you learned it and what still needs checking.

43 / 60
DEFINE THE PLAYING FIELD

Know the market you are actually entering.

Industry tells you the broad economic space. Category tells you the specific set of offers customers compare. Business model explains how the organisation creates and captures value. These labels answer different questions.

01 / SECTOR

The broad economic field

Large areas of economic activity, such as financial services, healthcare, education, agriculture, energy, media, transport or consumer goods.

02 / INDUSTRY

The business arena

A more defined group of organisations doing related work, such as banking, insurance, hospitals, online education, food manufacturing or logistics.

03 / CATEGORY

The comparison set

The kind of offer customers recognise and compare when choosing: digital banking, health insurance, online courses, skincare, quick-service food or business software.

04 / SUBCATEGORY

The narrower space

A more specific slice of the category, such as merchant payment gateways, children’s skincare, exam-preparation courses or same-day grocery delivery.

BUSINESS MODEL

How the organisation creates, delivers and earns value: subscription, marketplace, direct sales, service fees, licensing, transaction fees, manufacturing, distribution, franchising or a hybrid.

CUSTOMER / BUYING CONTEXT

Who pays, who uses, and how the decision happens: B2B, B2C, public sector, donor-funded, or a mix. This is separate from the industry and category.

WORKED EXAMPLE A merchant payments platform could sit in the financial services sector, within the financial technology industry, compete in the digital payments category, and specialise in merchant payment acceptance. It may earn through transaction fees and serve both businesses and consumers.

Ask four different questions: What economic field? What industry? What alternatives does the customer compare? How does this business earn?

44 / 60
LOOK FOR COMMERCIAL EVIDENCE

Who is spending money here, and what are they spending it on?

Look for signs of active demand: paid offers, pricing, transaction patterns, recurring purchases, reviews, category growth and the problems customers repeatedly pay to solve.

PAID OFFERSAre people paying for solutions already?
PRICE POINTSWhat are customers paying, and how often?
REVIEWSWhat do buyers praise or complain about?
REPEAT BEHAVIOURDoes the category encourage recurring use?
DISTRIBUTIONWhere are offers actually available?
MARKET DATAWhat do credible reports and public data show?
Attention is not the same as demand. Interest is not the same as a purchase.
45 / 60
COMPETITOR RESEARCH

Who else is solving the same customer problem?

Study direct competitors, indirect competitors and substitutes. A competitor may sell a similar product, solve the same problem differently, or compete for the same budget and attention.

Direct

Similar offer, similar customer, similar buying situation.

Indirect

Different offer, same customer need or desired outcome.

Substitute

Another way to solve the problem or spend the budget.

Do nothing

The customer delays, tolerates the problem or uses an existing workaround.

46 / 60
WHAT TO INVESTIGATE

Do not stop at their logo and Instagram grid.

Compare the offer, customer, price, positioning, proof, distribution, customer experience, reviews and the promises each competitor makes. Then look for patterns in what customers praise and complain about.

01Offer and value proposition
02Audience and use case
03Price and payment model
04Positioning and proof
05Distribution and experience
06Reviews, complaints and recurring themes
Competitor research is market intelligence, not imitation.
47 / 60
THE POSITIONING QUESTION

Different is better than better.

“Better quality” is easy to claim and difficult to own. A meaningful difference gives a specific customer a reason to choose you. It may come from the audience, access, experience, speed, specialisation, model or point of view.

Weak difference

“We have the best quality and customer service.”

Useful difference

“We deliver a specialised service for a clearly defined customer whose needs are poorly served by the standard options.”

A difference only matters when the customer values it.
48 / 60
LOOK FOR THE UNDERSERVED

Where are customers being underserved?

A gap is a hypothesis, not an automatic opportunity. Test whether people care, whether they will pay, whether the business can deliver, and whether the economics make sense.

PEOPLE CARE
Is the need meaningful?
PEOPLE PAY
Is there willingness to pay?
WE CAN DELIVER
Can the business serve it?
THE MODEL WORKS
Can it be commercially viable?
An unserved need may be unserved for a reason.

CUSTOMER SERVED

OFFER AND PRICE

What is being sold, how is it packaged, and what does it cost?

POSITIONING

What promise or point of difference does it communicate?

DISTRIBUTION

EVIDENCE AND GAP

METHODS
RESEARCH METHODS & APPLICATION

Show me the receipts.

Good research is a disciplined way of reducing uncertainty. It gives your recommendations somewhere to stand.

Google is a starting point, not a research strategy.
51 / 60
THE RESEARCH TOOLKIT / PRIMARY, SECONDARY & FIRST-PARTY DATA

Choose the tool that can answer the question.

Primary research is information you collect directly for this investigation. Secondary research is information that already exists. First-party analytics are behavioural records generated by your own channels. They are related, but they are not interchangeable.

01

PRIMARY RESEARCH

You go to people, watch behaviour or test an experience yourself.

INTERVIEWS & CONVERSATIONS
WhatsAppVoice calls, chats, customer follow-ups
ZoomRemote customer or founder interviews
Google MeetRecorded or live conversations, with consent
SURVEYS & QUESTIONNAIRES
Google FormsStructured responses and simple surveys
TypeformConversational survey experiences
SurveyMonkeySurvey design and response analysis
OBSERVATION, TESTING & FIELDWORK

Watch a customer complete a task, visit a store, observe service delivery, run a usability session, compare prototypes, or test two versions of an offer. Tools can include screen recordings, session notes and structured observation sheets.

02

SECONDARY RESEARCH

You analyse information collected or published by someone else.

PUBLIC CONVERSATIONS & CULTURE
RedditCommunities, complaints, language and workarounds
InstagramComments, reviews, creator and brand activity
TikTokPublic reactions, trends and category language
SEARCH, TRENDS & MARKET INTELLIGENCE
Google TrendsRelative search-interest patterns over time
AnswerThePublicDiscover questions and search phrases around a topic
StatistaPublished statistics and market reports
SimilarwebEstimated website and traffic intelligence
QUESTIONS & EXISTING MEDIA
YouTube / podcastsExisting interviews, reviews and expert discussions
Google ScholarAcademic papers and published studies

Use the questions as discovery clues. Validate them against customer conversations, search trends and actual buying behaviour. Search autocomplete can provide an additional free cross-check.

Google Analytics
FIRST-PARTY BEHAVIOURAL DATA

Your website or app analytics can show what visitors do on your own channels: acquisition sources, page activity, key events and drop-off. This is observed behaviour from your properties, not a substitute for asking why people behave that way.

CLASSIFICATION RULE: A podcast you listen to is secondary. A podcast-style interview you conduct with a customer is primary. Public Reddit or social posts are secondary. A conversation you initiate with a Reddit user for your study is primary. Google Trends shows relative interest, not exact search volume or sales.
52 / 60
ASK BETTER QUESTIONS

Ask about what people did, not only what they say they might do.

Use open questions. Ask for recent examples. Follow up on specifics. Avoid leading language. Listen for the words people use to describe the problem, the alternatives and the decision.

RECENTTell me about the last time this happened.
SPECIFICWhat did you do next?
ALTERNATIVESWhat else did you consider?
DECISIONWhat mattered most when choosing?
FRICTIONWhat nearly stopped you?
OUTCOMEHow did it work out?
“Tell me about the last time…” is often more useful than “Would you…?”
53 / 60
SORT WHAT YOU KNOW

An assumption, a finding and an insight are different things.

An assumption is something you believe but have not verified. A finding is what the evidence shows. An insight explains why a pattern matters. A recommendation proposes what the business should consider doing.

Assumption

“People in this age group prefer buying through Instagram.” Not yet verified.

Finding

“In 8 interviews, 6 participants said they discovered the brand through referrals.” A documented observation from a defined sample.

Insight

“Trust transferred through personal recommendations appears to reduce hesitation.” An interpretation of the pattern.

Recommendation

“Investigate how referrals influence acquisition before increasing paid spend.” A proposed next step.

USE AI WITH YOUR EYES OPEN

Treat every AI-generated claim as something to verify.

AI can help you move through research material faster. Before using a claim in your report, return to the original source and check what it actually says.

CHECK THE SOURCE

Open the original page, report, dataset or publication. Do not rely on an AI summary as your citation.

CHECK THE CLAIM

Confirm the wording, date, geography, sample and definition. Make sure the source supports the exact point you want to make.

CHECK THE CONTEXT

Look for limitations, missing information, commercial incentives and evidence that points in another direction.

RECORD THE RECEIPT

Save the source link, publication date, access date and the specific evidence you used.

If you cannot trace the claim to a credible source, leave it out or label it as unverified.

TURN INFORMATION INTO JUDGEMENT

Congratulations. You have data. Now tell me what it means.

A useful insight connects evidence to a business implication. It explains what is happening, why it matters, who it affects and what decision it could change.

WHAT
What did you find?
SO WHAT
Why does it matter?
FOR WHOM
Who is affected?
NOW WHAT
What decision follows?
A pile of links is not a research report.

Choose an existing business. Diagnose before you prescribe.

Pick a real business you know as a customer. In five minutes, identify what you would need to understand before recommending a marketing move. This is a diagnostic warm-up, not the Week 1 assessment.

BUSINESS

CUSTOMER

Who appears to buy it? What evidence do you have?

FRICTION

Where might a customer hesitate, struggle or abandon the process?

ALTERNATIVES

What else could the customer choose, including doing nothing?

MISSING EVIDENCE

What do you currently assume that you would need to verify?

FIRST QUESTION

What is the first question you would investigate, and why?

WEEK 1 ASSESSMENT / START HERE

WHAT YOUR REPORT MUST CONTAINASSESSMENT WORKSHEET / REPORT SECTIONS

Use these six sections to build your report.

Write your analysis in the fields. Link each important claim to evidence and carry your source records into the final submission.

01 BUSINESS OVERVIEW AND REVENUE MODEL

What does the business do, who pays, what do they pay for, and how does revenue happen?

02 OBJECTIVES AND CURRENT CONSTRAINTS

What business outcome matters, what is limiting it, and what evidence supports that diagnosis?

03 INDUSTRY AND COMPETITIVE ENVIRONMENT

Describe the category, market dynamics, competitors, substitutes and commercial signals.

04 CUSTOMER SEGMENTS AND BUYING BEHAVIOUR

Describe priority segments, needs, triggers, decision factors, barriers and buying journeys.

05 OFFER AND 4 PS ANALYSIS

Evaluate product, price, place and promotion against customer needs and business realities.

06 FINDINGS, GAPS AND PRIORITIES

Separate findings from interpretation. Identify the most credible opportunity and the next questions to test.

THE STANDARDASSESSMENT WORKSHEET / SOURCE LOG

Make it possible for someone else to check your work.

Include source links, dates accessed and screenshots where useful. Separate evidence from interpretation. Be specific about what you do not know. Do not present a guess as a fact.

Source trail

URL, publisher, date published if available, date accessed, relevant screenshot or excerpt.

Evidence labels

Fact, finding, inference, assumption or recommendation. Make the distinction visible.

Your evidence should make your reasoning independently checkable.
